articles.title: Maine buried 20,000 discarded tyres beneath a road to fight frost and spring mud, while turning a growing waste problem into an engineering solution
articles.summary: US News: Along a quiet stretch of road in Maine, engineers buried something most people would expect to see in a scrapyard rather than beneath their tyres: abo.
articles.body: Along a quiet stretch of road in Maine, engineers buried something most people would expect to see in a scrapyard rather than beneath their tyres: about 20,000 discarded car tyres. The unusual experiment was designed to tackle two problems at once. Maine’s roads face a difficult seasonal cycle, with winter freezing the ground and spring thaw turning it soft and unstable. Gravel roads can quickly develop ruts and potholes as vehicles pass over the weakened surface. At the same time, the state produces more than a million unwanted tyres each year, creating a growing waste problem with few easy outlets.University of Maine engineer Dana Humphrey wondered whether shredded tyres could become part of the solution. Cut into large chips and placed beneath a conventional gravel surface, the rubber acted differently from ordinary road fill. When spring arrived, the experimental section showed noticeably less frost penetration and deterioration than nearby parts of the road.Maine tested old tyres beneath roads to make them stronger in springMaine has a particularly large network of unpaved roads, many of them exposed to repeated cycles of freezing in winter and thawing in spring. As temperatures rise, water held in the ground can turn road surfaces soft. Heavy vehicles then make matters worse, leaving sections of gravel roads difficult to travel.The tyre-chip idea was developed by University of Maine civil engineer Dana Humphrey, who was investigating whether the unusual properties of shredded rubber could be put to work inside a road structure.The material was not being used as a replacement for the road surface. Instead, it formed a layer beneath conventional gravel. The chips were intended to change what happened below the surface, rather than provide the wearing surface on which vehicles travelled.20,000 tyres went beneath one Maine road for a winter testAs reported by Los Angeles Times, a section of Dingley Road in Richmond became the site of a winter-long experiment. About 20,000 discarded tyres were cut into pieces roughly 2 to 3 inches across. The pieces still contained their steel belts.They were spread across a 600-foot section of the road, forming a layer between about 6 and 12 inches thick. Gravel was then placed above them in successive layers, eventually creating a conventional-looking road surface.Reportedly, the experiment was closely monitored. More than 100 temperature sensors were installed at different depths within the roadbed by Robert A. Eaton of the US Army Corps of Engineers Cold Regions Research & Engineering Laboratory. The sensors were connected to computers in Hanover, New Hampshire, allowing temperatures inside the road structure to be recorded throughout the winter.By spring, the tyre-chip section was behaving differently from nearby portions made entirely with gravel. Frost had penetrated to roughly half the depth observed in the comparison sections, while the gravel-only portions deteriorated badly during the thaw.Why shredded tyres worked differently from ordinary gravelTyre chips have a physical advantage over ordinary road aggregate: they are much lighter. Gravel weighs about 125 pounds per cubic foot, whereas the tyre material used in the experiments weighed around 40 pounds.That difference can become important when large quantities of fill are needed. A lighter material places less weight on the soil below it, which makes the approach particularly interesting for construction on weak ground.Rubber also behaves differently from mineral soil when temperatures change. It does not transfer heat as readily, giving the chips an insulating quality. At the same time, the irregular pieces leave spaces through which water can move.The three characteristics: low weight, insulation and drainage made the material useful for more than just keeping frost out of a road.Engineers began testing tyre chips beyond road constructionHumphrey and two graduate students also began constructing a retaining wall on the University of Maine campus. The planned structure was about 15 feet high and was intended to explore whether tyre chips could serve as lightweight fill behind a wall.That application had implications for places where conventional earth fill puts substantial pressure on slopes or retaining structures. Humphrey suggested that the method could have uses on steep roads in Southern California, where reducing the weight of material placed against a hillside could be useful in managing problems associated with unstable slopes.The concept was different from using finely ground rubber in asphalt. Crumb rubber had already been incorporated into some highway paving, but it required a much more processed product and was considerably more expensive.For one mile of interstate resurfacing in Maine, the material reportedly accounted for about 6,000 tyres, at a cost exceeding $20 per tyre. Using larger tyre pieces as fill could consume far greater quantities without requiring the same degree of grinding.Maine had millions of old tyres with few places to goThe engineering experiment was taking place against a substantial waste problem. Maine residents were estimated to discard about 1.2 million tyres each year. Some ended up stored in large piles, including abandoned stockpiles that created environmental and fire concerns. Tyres can hold rainwater, providing places for mosquitoes to breed, while large tyre fires can burn for long periods and produce difficult-to-manage smoke.The state's recycling policy had also been shaped by legal and environmental problems surrounding two enormous tyre stockpiles. Government authorities were eventually placed in the position of dealing with the sites, adding pressure to find uses for tyres after disposal.For recyclers, however, finding an outlet was not necessarily the difficult part of collecting them. The market for products made from old tyres was still relatively small. In many cases, the disposal service itself generated more revenue than the sale of recycled material.Some tyres were already being burned for energy. Maine had waste-to-energy facilities that could use tyre chips, while a paper mill also used them as fuel. But preparing the material for combustion brought its own costs, particularly because the steel had to be removed as far as possible and the rubber needed to be cut into smaller pieces.The next test moved closer to a normal highwayThe Richmond experiment used a gravel surface, so it did not answer every question about how tyre chips would perform beneath an ordinary paved road.That was the purpose of a planned test in North Yarmouth. An asphalt-topped section of highway was due to be constructed later that summer, providing an opportunity to see whether the material could perform beneath a conventional pavement under traffic.Earlier tests had indicated that once the chips were compacted using ordinary road-building equipment, they could support the loads imposed by heavy lorries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Grandfather dies months after confronting burglars at Helmshore home
articles.summary: Gordon Nicholass, 85, was the victim of a burglary at his home, say Lancashire Police.
articles.body:
An 85-year-old grandfather has died more than four months after confronting burglars who broke into his home.

Gordon Nicholass was the victim of a burglary at about 03:00 BST on 29 April at his home in the village of Helmshore, Lancashire.

Lancashire Police said he was assaulted and suffered injuries to his head and cuts to his face when he confronted the burglars. He was treated in hospital and sent home, but was later taken back to hospital and died on 12 August.

Post-mortem tests have been carried out, but further inquiries are being made to establish if the assault was a cause or contributory factor, police said. His family added: "Gordon was a wonderful husband, dad and granddad."

They added in a tribute: "He was a lifelong motorcycle enthusiast and well known for his engineering skills.

"He was always there to do anything for anyone - family, friends even strangers, you name it!"

They described him as "mister fix it" who was a "jack of all trades".

His family added: "We will all miss him dearly."

Police were called shortly before 03:00 GMT on 29 April after the break-in on Moss Close in the village.

The offenders broke in and assaulted Nicholass who lived at the address with his wife.

Extensive damage was caused to the property during the burglary but it did not appear that anything was taken.

Police said they believed the attack might "have been targeted".

Det Chief Insp Jill Vescovi said: "First and foremost my thoughts are with Gordon's family and loved ones.

"We will continue to offer them any support they need at this time."

articles.title: My family fled the ‘butchers’ in Iran 50 years ago. We can’t give them what they want
articles.summary: On Tuesday, Aug. 25, Trump announced the U.S. Navy cleared every Iranian mine from the Strait of Hormuz, but the regime's attrition strategy looms.
articles.body: On Tuesday, Aug. 25, President Donald Trump announced that the U.S. Navy has removed or detonated every Iranian mine in the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz. Tankers are moving again, gas prices should finally start to ease and Washington will be tempted to exhale. That would be a mistake. It took the most powerful navy on Earth six months to undo Tehran’s damage to the strait. The 60-day negotiating window produced nothing; Iran's foreign ministry said the deadline "essentially has no relevance," and the regime that just lost this round is already winding the next clock. I know that clock. My family lived under it before we fled Iran, a Jewish family that watched the revolution turn our homeland into a place where we could no longer safely exist. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and the rest of the regime leadership are not trying to beat the American military; they are trying to outlast the American taxpayer, and the regime is banking its survival on exactly that. TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS A year after Operation Midnight Hammer and the 12-Day War showed the world what American power can do in a matter of days, the American public’s worst fear is materializing anyway: a drawn-out conflict. The strait may be reopening, but the squeeze of the past six months reached pocketbooks nationwide, midterm elections are approaching and Washington is debating how, and how fast, to prosecute this war. The longer this war runs, the more the Iranian regime gains. The only question that matters is whether America fights the war Tehran designed or the war America can win. Since 1979, the dictatorship has run the same play, which U.S. officials have long described as "deception, defiance and delay." Buy time, bleed the adversary, survive to rebuild. The arithmetic of this war was built for that play. Tehran fields a Shahed suicide drone for about $20,000; America answers with Patriot interceptors at roughly $4 million each. Iran maintains the capacity to manufacture an estimated 10,000 drones a month, has begun rebuilding its missile facilities, and is moving valuable assets underground. Every truce and every pause becomes a rearmament window for Iran. Tehran is not waiting alone. The regime signed a 20-year strategic partnership with Russia, is receiving more than a thousand tons of missile-making chemicals from China, and collaborates on missile technology with North Korea. Each arrangement lowers what it costs the ayatollah to keep firing, which means our gravest geopolitical rivals are helping underwrite the missiles aimed at us. The rest of the bill lands on Iran’s neighbors, as the regime strikes airports, shipping and commercial districts across the Gulf states, from Dubai to Doha, to spread the pain and build pressure for American concessions. IRAN TAPS FINANCIAL LIFELINE, RUSSIAN ARMS AS TRUMP ESCALATES 'CRUSHING' ECONOMIC WARFARE A U.N. fact-finding mission found Iran responsible for the systematic rape and brutalization of women. Iran’s laws make homosexuality punishable by death, and the regime persecutes ethnic and religious minorities as policy. My family was one of those minorities. My mother pulled my brother and me out of Iran because being Jewish there had become dangerous, and she rebuilt our lives in America from nothing. In January, after a nationwide uprising, the regime reportedly murdered more than 30,000 people, most of them students and young people, in just two days. It has carried out nearly a thousand executions since. Those are my people, Jewish and Muslim alike. I am now a mother of four daughters, and I think about the mothers in Tehran raising girls under a regime that treats their bodies as state property. Every day this regime survives, more of them die waiting for the world to act. IRAN’S KILLER DRONES INCREASE SLAUGHTER IN SUDAN AMID WORLD’S FORGOTTEN WAR The violence has never been limited to its own captive citizens. Iran’s proxies killed 241 U.S. service members in the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing and at least 603 more in Iraq, by the Pentagon’s own count. The regime has funded anti-Israel protesters inside America, interfered in our elections, and plotted to assassinate American officials, including the president. I have seen that campaign up close. My daughter was a student at Columbia when the encampments took over campus, and she testified before Congress about what Jewish students were facing. The regime's reach into American institutions is not abstract to my family. For Tehran, delay is not a pause. It is an opportunity to extract more blood and damage America from within. Some in Washington counsel patience. The blockade is biting, they note, and U.S. intelligence has assessed the regime can withstand roughly 90 to 120 more days. But two things can be true at once. The blockade is hurting the regime and the regime does not care. My family was one of those minorities. My mother pulled my brother and me out of Iran because being Jewish there had become dangerous, and she rebuilt our lives in America from nothing. The ayatollah will starve his own people, shake down his neighbors and cut backroom deals with Moscow and Beijing before he yields. Meanwhile, every passing day writes another costly line in America’s ledger. A war of attrition is the one war this regime can win, because it built the war that way on purpose. An accommodation, which leaves the regime its missiles, its nuclear ambitions and its proxies, and buys a pause, which they will spend preparing the next round. Or a decisive end to the war on America’s terms. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Simply weakening the regime without ending it just kicks the can down the road. The United States must destroy the regime’s military-industrial capacity, cripple the energy infrastructure that bankrolls the Revolutionary Guard and break its ability to crush the Iranian people who keep rising against it. My family fled the butchers who stole my country nearly five decades ago, and I have spent every year since watching the world try to manage, contain and negotiate with them. The Iranian people are not our enemy; they are the regime’s first hostages. America proved in Operation Midnight Hammer what the most powerful military in human history can do, and it is our job to finish the job.

articles.title: The data center fight could decide the next president and cost America the AI race
articles.summary: Rising electric bills and data center construction spark bipartisan pushback from governors, but restricting AI infrastructure could cost America its lead.
articles.body: It’s the fall of 2028. A debate moderator turns to two presidential nominees who spent their governorships fighting over data centers. "China’s AI lead is now a fact," she says. "In 2026, you decided to restrict data-center construction, and the machinist in Youngstown, Ohio, watched his job follow the servers to the Gulf. What do you tell him? Which of your policies would you take back?" That reckoning is two years away, but the choices that will decide it are being made now. Rising electric bills deserve a real fix, but not one rushed for political expediency that leaves the people it’s meant to help worse off down the road. The pressure to do something is building. Gary Elder retired to Lewisport, Ky., on a fixed income that makes any bill feel precarious. At a Public Service Commission hearing in Hancock County this July, the 69-year-old told regulators he was worried a 500-megawatt data center proposed nearby could push his electric bill toward $1,000 or more. Elder represents seven in 10 Americans who oppose a data center in their own backyard. And when politicians sense trouble, they move fast. FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS By August, Pennsylvania Democrat Gov. Josh Shapiro and Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, two governors who spent recent years courting hyperscale data centers, were both moving the other way. Shapiro signed an executive order he called the "strictest guardrails in the nation." Abbott froze new grid connections pending a statewide audit. New York Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul went further, pausing environmental permits for a year, and Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis guaranteed local governments’ authority to reject data centers. Republicans and Democrats are arriving at the same anxiety from different directions. FROM NEW YORK TO TEXAS, STATES SHOULD RESPECT LOCAL CONTROL ON DATA CENTERS In contrast, President Donald Trump has been the most unambiguous pro-buildout voice in the country, calling Abbott’s freeze a "mistake," while Senate Republicans have privately warned the issue could cost them Ohio’s Senate seat, where Trump-endorsed Sen. Jon Husted trails as "the face of data centers." The same dynamic is now repeating in the state’s gubernatorial race with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy calling for a moratorium of his own, and Democrat Amy Acton countering with hers. For any ambitious politician eyeing 2028, there is little downside to running as the candidate who stood for cutting electric bills and considerable risk in being the one who has to explain why America’s compute lead matters. TRUMP HEADS TOWARD UNLIKELY CLASH WITH CLOSE ALLY OVER FUTURE OF MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR INDUSTRY Data centers are not just computer warehouses. They are the physical foundation of artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, scientific research, autonomous systems and, increasingly, national-security capabilities. Goldman Sachs estimates that U.S. AI-related investment will approach $600 billion in 2026. But every gigawatt of capacity America fails to build can flow to countries with faster permitting, cheaper power or more predictable policy, taking construction jobs, supply-chain work and the tax base with it. Ironically, many of this year’s stalled projects aren’t zoning fights at all. They’re running into a more fundamental constraint: scarce high-voltage transformers, a bottleneck that exists with or without protests. The strategic vulnerability is that China accounts for roughly 60% of global transformer production capacity. Saudi Arabia’s $100 billion HUMAIN program, the UAE’s Stargate and a Japan buildout backed by Gulf sovereign wealth are courting the same capital American localities are turning away. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE So how do we address legitimate concerns while keeping our eye on the strategic imperative of becoming the "AI capital of the world," as Trump put it? Start by recognizing what this fight is actually about. Americans don’t oppose data centers; they oppose feeling like someone else gets the benefit while they get the bill. This shouldn’t be treated as us vs them, but as a solvable problem that comes down to three practical questions: where the power gets built, who pays for it and how fast the permits move. DATA CENTERS FORGOT THE CONSUMER — AND THAT COULD COST AMERICA THE AI RACE Data centers should pay the incremental cost of the electricity infrastructure they require, enter transparent power agreements, invest in new generation and storage where feasible and use energy- and water-efficient technologies. Communities should have meaningful input, and governments should tie tax incentives to measurable economic benefits. For any ambitious politician eyeing 2028, there is little downside to running as the candidate who stood for cutting electric bills and considerable risk in being the one who has to explain why America’s compute lead matters. Done right, this isn’t just fair, it works. Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy found that large loads haven’t been the principal driver of rising rates, and in some places with the highest demand growth, prices have actually fallen, provided supply, cost allocation and tariff design are sound. AMERICA NEEDS AI TO SURVIVE. WORKING FAMILIES ALSO NEED TO SURVIVE IT States should also encourage data centers to locate where power is abundant, as West Virginia is doing. Its leaders view data centers as critical infrastructure and are positioning abundant energy, microgrids and proximity to population centers as advantages. Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey has described the approach as a 20-year strategy, while Google has announced a multibillion-dollar project there. That’s the model America should pursue: more capacity, in more places, with smarter rules. THE WAR ON DATA CENTERS JEOPARDIZES OUR ECONOMY AND NATIONAL SECURITY Technology companies have a role, too. In March, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to bring or buy power for their facilities and cover required infrastructure upgrades rather than shift those costs onto households. Get that sequencing right, and there’s a benefit even the buildout critics tend to overlook: the trades. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Building a data-center campus requires a large skilled workforce, including electricians, pipefitters and high-voltage crews. Meta’s president estimates the U.S. could need roughly 500,000 additional electricians alone to support the AI infrastructure buildout. Microsoft’s president has called the electrician shortage the company’s biggest constraint. That’s why Google, Microsoft and the electrical workers’ union are pouring money into apprenticeships that lead to well-paying careers without student debt. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We don’t have to choose between Gary Elder’s electric bill and America’s technological lead. We can do both. When those presidential nominees face the data-center question in 2028, they can say: "We kept bills affordable while keeping America in the lead." CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM LEN KHODORKOVSKY

articles.title: Hungry bears are entering homes, shops and neighbourhoods across the US; here’s what is driving the alarming trend
articles.summary: World News: A hungry pair of young black bears recently wandered into a home in Granby, Colorado, startling a resident who found them standing in his hallway. The.
articles.body: A hungry pair of young black bears recently wandered into a home in Granby, Colorado, startling a resident who found them standing in his hallway. The animals eventually bolted through the front door, but the unusual intrusion is part of a much larger pattern unfolding across the American West. Reuters reported that bear sightings and conflicts are rising sharply as severe drought leaves wild animals struggling to find food. Bears have been spotted in increasingly unlikely places, from homes and shops to school areas and busy neighbourhoods. In Colorado alone, wildlife officials have recorded more than 7,000 bear sightings in 2026, already surpassing the state’s previous full-year record of about 5,400 sightings in 2019.A severe drought is leaving bears hungryAt the heart of the problem is an unusually dry year across the western US. The region experienced an exceptionally dry winter, followed by drought conditions that have reduced the availability of plants, grasses, berries and nuts, foods that make up roughly 90% of a bear’s natural diet, according to experts and state wildlife agencies cited by Reuters.That shortage is forcing bears to travel farther and take greater risks in their search for calories. And once they reach human settlements, they can find an irresistible alternative: garbage, pet food, bird seed, fruit trees and other easily accessible sources of food. Bears have an exceptionally strong sense of smell, making residential areas particularly attractive when natural food is scarce.From forests to kitchens and shopsThe consequences are increasingly visible. In Granby, bears were spotted not only inside a home but also in a vape shop. In Santa Fe, New Mexico, a bear was seen near a school, while another climbed a tree close to a farmers market in Denver. A bear cub also recently wandered into a restaurant in Aspen.Colorado Parks and Wildlife received 6,129 reports of bear sightings and conflicts between January 1 and August 13, almost double the 3,115 reports recorded during the same period last year. The agency has also reported a significant increase in property damage linked to bears searching for food. The problem isn’t limited to Colorado. Wildlife authorities have reported increasing conflicts in states including New Mexico, Utah, Montana and California.More bears are also living near peopleDrought is only one part of the story. Decades of development have pushed homes and communities into areas that were once bear habitat. At the same time, conservation efforts have helped bear populations recover in several parts of the US.Colorado is now home to an estimated 17,000 to 20,000 black bears, according to state authorities. The state’s human population has also more than doubled over the past 50 years, increasing the amount of overlap between people and bears. This means bears are not necessarily moving into entirely unfamiliar territory. In many cases, human settlements have expanded into landscapes the animals historically used to forage.The encounters can turn deadlyMost bear encounters do not result in attacks, and experts stress that bears generally avoid humans. But when animals become accustomed to finding food around people, the risk of conflict increases.The number of bears dying as a result of these encounters is also climbing. New Mexico authorities have killed 187 bears this year, the state’s highest number since 2011, while Utah has euthanised 39 bears, already a record for a full year. In Montana, 24 grizzlies have died this year, mostly after conflicts involving livestock or people or after being hit by vehicles.New Mexico also recorded its first fatal bear attack in 25 years this month, while a man was killed by a grizzly in Montana’s Glacier National Park in May. Fatal bear attacks, however, remain rare across the western US.Why the problem could get worseWildlife experts are particularly concerned about the coming months. Bears normally need to consume large amounts of food before winter to build up fat reserves for hibernation. With natural food supplies already depleted, they could become even more dependent on human settlements.Experts also warn that prolonged drought and warmer winters could eventually alter traditional hibernation patterns and make bears increasingly accustomed to human food. For residents, wildlife officials recommend keeping garbage secured in bear-resistant containers, bringing bins out only on collection days, removing bird feeders and keeping pet food and barbecue grills away from bears.The message from wildlife experts is simple: don’t feed a hungry bear, even if you think you’re helping. Once a bear learns that humans are a reliable source of food, it may keep returning, even after conditions in the wild improve.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kazakhstan’s Tokayev appoints longtime adviser as vice president
articles.summary: Erlan Karin has served as a top ⁠⁠aide to Tokayev since he took over the presidency in 2019.
articles.body:
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has appointed longtime adviser Erlan Karin as vice president, the office ‌‌created under a new constitution adopted earlier this year.

The move on Monday makes Karin, who has served as a top ⁠⁠aide to Tokayev since taking over the presidency in 2019, first in line to succeed him as leader of the Central Asian country.

Tokayev described Karin as an experienced public servant with extensive knowledge of state governance, local media reported.

“He has worked in the system of public administration for many years. One can say that he is a person of broad outlook, with rich experience and a true patriot,” Tokayev was quoted as saying.

The 50-year-old has a background in “counter-terrorism” and has ⁠⁠positioned himself as a key figure in promoting Tokayev’s ideology, which he has dubbed “New Kazakhstan”.

Tokayev also proposed reappointing Olzhas Bektenov as prime minister, a position ⁠⁠he has held since 2024.

Both appointments were swiftly approved by parliament, which is dominated ⁠⁠by the pro-Tokayev Adilet party.

Tokayev, 73, ‌‌is eligible to run for another seven-year term as president under the new constitution, according to Kazakhstan’s supreme court. His current term ends in 2029. presidents are otherwise limited to a single term in office under Kazakh basic law.

Tokayev, a ⁠⁠former Soviet diplomat and top United Nations official, took office as the chosen successor of Nursultan Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan’s founding president, who ruled from 1991 to 2019.

Tokayev broke from ‌‌his predecessor, whom he had served as prime minister and foreign minister, in 2022 after a bout of nationwide unrest that left ‌‌hundreds ‌‌dead and which he cast as a coup attempt by Nazarbayev-era figures.

Kazakhstan is a major exporter of energy and minerals, including uranium for nuclear power, and maintains warm ties with Russia, the West and China.

articles.title: Iran attacks Jordan, UAE after US bombs Larak Island: What’s the latest?
articles.summary: The retaliatory attacks came after the US targeted two Iranian launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Iran says it has attacked US bases in Jordan and US military assets in the United Arab Emirates in retaliation for strikes on Larak Island in the first active exchange between the two sides since late July.

The Iranian response came after the United States claimed to have hit two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. A US official told Al Jazeera Arabic following the attack that the launchers were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines towards the waterway.

In his first comments since the attack, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was “not looking for war”, but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression” either.

Iran “will give a decisive response to the aggressors” if attacked, Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by the Iranian news agency Fars. “Instability and unrest in the region are not in the interest of any country and will challenge everyone.”

Here’s what we know so far and what could happen to the diplomatic efforts to end the six-month-old war that has disrupted global oil supply and jolted the global economy.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the US attacks on Sunday night had killed and wounded several Iranian soldiers and civilians.

Iran’s Fars news agency also reported IRGC spokesperson Sardar Mohebi accusing the US of making “a strategic and fatal mistake” for which it will face consequences “in both the economic and military arenas”.

But on Monday morning, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a post on X that the IRGC’s statement that the attack on Larak Island was an “act of aggression” was false, and said forces took “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz”.

“In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce,” it added on X.

US President Donald Trump on Monday claimed that Kharg Island is being “blown to smithereens” in a post on his Truth Social platform. Iran has yet to comment on Trump’s claims.

Last week, the US president said all mines ‌had been detonated or removed from the waterway, and Iran was told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the US strike on Larak Island in a statement as a “direct violation of national sovereignty and territorial integrity”.

It added the attack caused civilian and military casualties.

Shortly after the US strikes, the IRGC said a combined missile and drone operation targeted the King Hussein and Al Azraq US military bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.

The strikes “destroyed the technical and repair infrastructure, as well as the enemy fighter deployment sites”, causing significant damage, the IRGC said in a statement.

Tehran dubbed the strikes on Jordan as “a legitimate exercise of self-defence” under the UN Charter.

“Iranian armed forces launched retaliatory missile strikes against US military positions in Jordan, targeting bases identified as the launching ground for a Sunday night attack on Larak Island,” the statement said.

“Aggression and crimes will not solve the enemy’s desperation in attempting to weaken the Islamic Republic’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and every attack will be met with even more devastating responses.”

At the same time, a US official told Al Jazeera Arabic that they were able to intercept Iran’s attacks against Jordan, adding that “the missile attack on US forces in Jordan proves that Iran is no longer the power it once was”.

They added that Tehran had launched medium-range ballistic missiles towards Jordan.

And in a statement released on Monday, Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles fired by Iran. “Air defence systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the Kingdom’s airspace at dawn today,” read the statement, quoting the army’s spokesperson.

Early on Monday morning, Iran’s Fars and Mehr news agencies cited a statement from the IRGC that said its air defences had intercepted “a long-range American MQ9 drone” over the Strait of Hormuz, which then fell into the Gulf.

Harlan Ullman, a retired US senior naval officer, told Al Jazeera that the attacks on Jordan were a “political statement”.

“They are signalling to Jordan that it is a target,” he said.

“It is a politically significant target,” he said, adding that the Iranian attack was carried out “with malice aforethought, not necessarily to impose damage on the Americans, but to tell the Jordanians: Are you sure you want to support the Americans?”

Iran’s army also said in a statement carried by Iranian news agencies that dozens of drones were launched at US military assets at the Al Menhad airbase in the UAE.

It said the attack targeted ⁠locations where US forces ⁠and helicopters were stationed at ⁠the base, adding that it was revenge for members of the IRGC and civilians who had been killed during the attack on Larak Island.

On Monday morning, the UAE’s Ministry of Defence said its air force responded to a drone over its territorial waters, approaching from Iran. The ministry, however, rejected Iranian claims that its airbase was targeted.

UAE’s ministry of foreign affairs “strongly condemned the Iranian aggression” in a post on X.

Still, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it would respond decisively to any further military aggression and said the US and parties supporting its actions were fully responsible for any escalation.

Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Manuel Rapalo explained that the tit-for-tat exchanges are the scenario that US diplomats who have been working with other countries to bring a diplomatic off-ramp did not want.

“The Trump administration has been signalling over the course of the last week that talks have deteriorated, that diplomacy has lost momentum, and we have seen that shift in strategy away from kinetic action and towards economic pressure,” Rapalo said.

“This is something that the treasury secretary spoke about specifically on Sunday, saying that there would be more sanctions coming up in the next few days,” he said, referring to economic sanctions targeting entities accused of doing business with Iran.

Last week, the US announced the latest sanctions on Iran in what officials called an “economic D-Day” and officially named “Operation Economic Outcast”, as Washington intensifies pressure on Tehran six months into the war.

Tehran, which has been under US sanctions for decades, says the new economic pressure will fail and shows that the US’s military approach has not worked.

articles.title: Dolly Parton laid to rest alongside husband in Nashville
articles.summary: A private family funeral is held for the singer who died on Tuesday at the age of 80.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, the music legend's great-niece has said.

The singer had a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, following her death earlier in the week at the age of 80.

She has been placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city.

Lainey Parton posted an emotional tribute a day after the burial, saying: "It still doesn't feel real that she's gone. I'm going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there."

She referred to Parton as "granny" and wrote: "Because she couldn't have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I'll forever be grateful for that."

Lainey remembered: "From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn't do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself."

Dolly Parton's dad couldn't read - it inspired her to send books to millions of children

'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton

Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy

Lainey also remembered how Parton had supported her through beauty school, explaining: "She didn't just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there."

She thanked those who have sent messages and flowers.

"I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny," she added. "Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything. I love you, Granny. Always."

An obituary posted by Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum remembered "her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family".

It continued: "Dolly Parton's legacy is one of love, kindness, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place."

It added: "In lieu of flowers, the family asks for donations to be made to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library." The Imagination Library was Parton's scheme to send free books to young children.

Amelia Young, a reporter for Nashville's NewsChannel 5, posted photos of flowers and a book of condolence at the tomb, which features a brass plaque showing Parton and Dean's names and engravings of their childhood homes.

On Saturday, one of Parton's nieces, Jada Star, performed as part of a tribute concert at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry House, regarded as the home of country music.

Star performed her song The Orchard, which she recorded with her aunt in 2024 on the album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.

"I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have," Star posted before the performance alongside a broken heart emoji. "I do not take this honor lightly."

Country superstar Jelly Roll made a surprise appearance during the event's finale - a group performance of Parton's 9 to 5 - while other participants included Carly Pearce, who has gone from being a performer at Parton's Dollywood theme park to a Grammy-winning singer.

Meanwhile, Tennessee's governor has announced plans to name Nashville International Airport after Parton.

In the UK, 9 to 5 is on course to be number one in the singles chart this week, according to the Official Chart Company, after fans streamed it in big numbers following Parton's death.

However, its streaming numbers have begun to decline, meaning it may not remain in the number one spot when the final chart is announced on Friday.

articles.title: In 1973, Christopher Cadbury funded the £40,000 purchase of a Seychelles island stripped for coconuts and seabird eggs; today over 1 million seabirds breed there each year
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For decades, the small island of Aride in the Seychelles was treated less as a wildlife sanctuary and more as a source of income. Its forests were cle.
articles.body: For decades, the small island of Aride in the Seychelles was treated less as a wildlife sanctuary and more as a source of income. Its forests were cleared for cultivation, coconut plantations covered parts of the island and its seabirds became a resource that could be harvested. Sooty tern eggs, in particular, were collected in huge numbers and shipped to other islands. Then, in 1973, British conservationist Christopher Cadbury stepped in.Cadbury, a member of the family behind the Cadbury chocolate company, provided £40,000 to enable the Society for the Promotion of Nature Reserves, now the Royal Society of Wildlife Trusts, to acquire Aride and protect it as a nature reserve. That sum would be equivalent to almost £1 million today, according to Silhouette, the Air Seychelles magazine. More than five decades later, the 74-hectare island has become one of the most important seabird colonies in the Indian Ocean. Around one million breeding seabirds belonging to 10 species are now associated with Aride, while its restored forests provide habitat for endemic birds, reptiles and plants. The transformation is striking because Aride was far from untouched when Cadbury helped secure its future.From exploitation to protectionAride is the northernmost of the granitic Seychelles islands and lies roughly 10 km from Praslin. Its landscape was dramatically altered during the period when the island was commercially exploited.Research published in Bird Conservation International records that Aride was once a coconut plantation. Vegetation on the hills was also repeatedly cleared to create suitable breeding grounds for Sooty Terns, whose eggs were harvested. The coconut plantation was eventually removed and native vegetation was gradually restored after the island was purchased in 1973.The scale of egg collection had been enormous. Historical records show that between 1948 and 1967, an estimated 171 to 173 cases of Sooty tern eggs were exported from Aride every year on average. In 1954 alone, as many as 312 cases, containing about 225,000 eggs, were harvested. Commercial egg collection finally stopped in 1967.The island had also suffered from the introduction of animals such as cats. Its original forest had been cleared and seabird eggs were collected and transported to Praslin. Yet Aride had one extraordinary advantage: rats never reached the island. Its lack of streams also made it less attractive to permanent settlement, while difficult landings limited access. Those factors helped preserve a foundation from which the island's ecosystem could eventually recover.A different kind of investmentCadbury recognised that potential and invested in protecting an ecosystem. After the acquisition, conservation efforts began to reverse decades of ecological damage. Coconut palms were removed and native trees were replanted. The vegetation on the island gradually recovered, creating habitat for species that had disappeared or declined.Aride was subsequently given legal protection as a Special Reserve under Seychelles law. Sources differ on the exact year of the designation, with conservation records citing 1975, while other accounts record the formal Special Reserve status as 1979.The management of the island eventually moved into local hands. The Island Conservation Society, a Seychelles-based conservation organisation, took over responsibility for managing Aride, and today its conservation staff are the only permanent inhabitants of the island.An island ruled by birdsToday, Aride supports approximately one million breeding seabirds across 10 species, making it one of the most significant seabird colonies in the Indian Ocean. The island is particularly important because its value is not limited to sheer numbers. It supports several species that are endemic to the Seychelles, meaning they are found nowhere else in the world.Among them is the Seychelles magpie-robin, a bird that once came dangerously close to extinction. A 2016 study in Bird Conservation International notes that the species had fallen to just 12 individuals on a single island in 1960. By 2015, intensive conservation programmes had helped increase its population to around 280 birds across five islands. Aride is among the islands involved in the species' recovery programme.The island also provides habitat for Seychelles fodies, Seychelles blue pigeons and Seychelles sunbirds, along with reptiles and a remarkable variety of plant life. The Key Biodiversity Areas database records about 100 vascular plant species on Aride, including species of particular conservation importance. Its importance extends beyond land. The protected area includes marine habitat around the island, adding another layer to its ecological significance.What £40,000 changedThe story of Aride is ultimately about what can happen when land is valued for something beyond its immediate commercial potential. In the early 20th century, seabirds were a resource to be harvested and forests were cleared for plantations. By 1973, the island had already endured decades of exploitation. Cadbury's intervention changed its trajectory.Instead of another plantation, Aride became a protected refuge. Instead of eggs being removed by the thousands, seabirds were allowed to breed. Instead of cleared hillsides, native vegetation returned. The transformation did not happen overnight. It required decades of habitat restoration, monitoring and protection. But the result is an ecosystem where wildlife has reclaimed the island on a remarkable scale.More than 50 years after Christopher Cadbury helped secure Aride for conservation, the island is no longer defined by what humans can extract from it. It is defined by what can survive there. And every year, roughly a million breeding seabirds provide perhaps the clearest measure of how dramatically that decision changed the island's future.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: JKIA strike: Passengers stranded as strike disrupts flights at Kenya's main airport
articles.summary: Kenya Airways says the strike has caused delays of more than six hours, with some flights cancelled.
articles.body:
Hundreds of passengers were stranded at Kenya's main airport in the capital, Nairobi, as flight disruptions continued for the second day amid a workers' strike.

Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) is a key regional transport hub.

On Sunday, the airports authority and the national carrier, Kenya Airways, warned departing flights may be delayed.

A new round of talks between unions and airport managers was due to take place on Monday, although discussions broke up a day earlier without agreement.

Aviation sector workers are on a nationwide go-slow strike to demand better working conditions and the implementation of a previously agreed deal.

Those hoping to get on a flight have been stuck at JKIA, with some spending the night in and around the check-in areas waiting for news.

Kenya Airways said in its latest update that due to "the industrial action by air traffic control workers", it is experiencing delays of more than six hours, and the flight backlog has forced it to cancel some departures.

It has apologised for the disruption and said passengers who would like to change or reschedule their flights could do so without a penalty.

Flight tracking website Flightradar24 showed a host of delayed, cancelled or diverted flights.

RwandAir said on Monday that it had cancelled two flights due to the ongoing "operational constraints affecting air traffic control services" at the airport. This followed earlier cancellations on Sunday.

Mendel Goldman, who was travelling to a wedding in Florida, told the Reuters news agency that his flight had been cancelled, after several delays.

He said he had been waiting for 12 hours.

"The earliest flight they can get us is only tomorrow night, so we've got to wait.

"We're going to try and make most of it, but in the meantime, I've been here for 12 hours now, waiting in the airport," he said.

William Obino, a 22-year-old traveller told the AFP news agency: "Nothing is happening, updates are reaching us late. It's ruining our itinerary."

The strike comes after a two-day dispute in February over collective bargaining and the use of volunteers at the airport.

Union officials said they took industrial action because concerns remained unresolved.

The main airport in Nairobi is one of the busiest hubs in the region and serves as a key gateway between the continent and the rest of the world. Last year, it handled about nine million passengers, according to the Kenyan authorities.

It has however seen multiple strikes in recent years as workers push for better conditions.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Monday categorically rejected a ruling by World Bank-constituted Court of Arbitration on Indus Water Treaty, terming it an "illegally constituted" organisation.In a statement, MEA said that New Delhi's decision to put the water treaty with Pakistan in abeyance "will remain in force.""This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body," the ministry said."India has never recognised the existence in law of this illegally-constituted and so-called Court of Arbitration, and has consistently maintained that the very establishment of this alleged arbitral body constitutes a grave violation of the Indus Waters Treaty. articles.title: Dungannon: Child in 'stable condition' as police continue murder investigation
articles.summary: The body of a 61-year-old man was found alongside his injured daughter and wife at a property in Lisnahull Road at about 11:00 BST on Saturday.
articles.body:
An eight-year-old girl is in a stable condition and a 16-year-old has been arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after an incident in Dungannon on Saturday .

The body of a 61-year-old man was found alongside his injured daughter at a house in Lisnahull Road at about 11:00 BST.

The man's wife, 48, who sustained non-life threatening injuries during the incident, has been released from hospital.

Police said detectives have been granted a court extension for a further 36 hours to question the teenager.

BBC News NI understands the man who died was from Guinea-Bissau, but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than two decades.

Speaking to the media on Monday, PSNI Supt Peter Stevenson said police received a report on Saturday morning from a member of the public about an ongoing disturbance at the house.

"Officers arrived short time later and discovered the body of a man, aged 61, his 48-year-old wife, who sustained non life threatening injuries, and their severely injured eight-year-old daughter," Stevenson said.

He said officers immediately commenced first aid on the woman and girl.

"I am in no doubt their quick actions gave the young girl a fighting chance at survival," Stevenson said, adding that she is now in a stable condition in hospital.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said they received a 999 call at 11:08 on Saturday, following reports of an incident.

They dispatched a helicopter crew, three emergency crews, one advanced care paramedic, two ambulance officers and one HART (Hazardous Area Response Team) crew to the scene.

"First and foremost, I want to express my sympathies to the loved ones of this family who will inevitably be struggling to come to terms with this horrendous news," Stevenson said.

He said specialist officers are supporting the wider family circle.

The public is being asked not to speculate on the case.

"I want to repeat that we do not believe there is an ongoing risk to the public. At this stage we are not looking for anyone else in connection with this investigation," Stevenson said.

He said the public will continue to see an increased police presence in the area.

"We understand the public interest and concern. We will continue to bring updates as our investigation progresses," he said.

Early support has been provided to officers who attended the scene, according to Stevenson, who said their "trauma-focused care will continue".

articles.title: Sir Mel Stride replaced as shadow chancellor amid Conservatives reshuffle
articles.summary: Andrew Griffith will take over the role as part of Kemi Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle.
articles.body:
Andrew Griffith has replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor as part of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's reshuffle of her top team.

Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary amid the ongoing shake-up.

Badenoch is forming a new shadow cabinet before the party's conference in October.

Badenoch paid tribute to Sir Mel's work as shadow chancellor saying he help the party rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition.

A senior Conservative source said: "Kemi is changing the way the Conservative Party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility."

Sir Mel, who was appointed to the role following Badenoch's leadership election in 2024, described his time in the senior Tory role as a "great honour".

"I am now looking forward to continuing to make a real contribution to the Conservative team in Parliament and beyond, to build and amplify our vision for Britain, from the back benches."

New shadow chancellor Griffith said the Tories will deliver "an economic revolution" with lower taxes, Britain drilling again to bring energy costs down, slashing red tape and Labour's Employment Rights Act.

"The Conservatives will always back the risk-takers and wealth creators who deliver growth, investment and jobs," he said.

A senior Conservative source described Griffith as a "no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience".

Before he became MP for Arundel and South Downs in 2019, Griffith served as a top executive at Sky and as chairman of Just Eat.

Badenoch will also need to select a new shadow health secretary after Stuart Andrew confirmed he will be returning to the backbenches.

Dame Priti, who had been shadow foreign secretary since 2024, said she will take on a new international role strenghtening the Tories relationship with sister parties and centre-right movements abroad.

The Warragul, Victoria, native started saving for property at age 16 after discussions with her father Luke, who bought his first home at 18. Real Estate (dot) com news site reported that she purchased a plot of land in her hometown and built a house on it three years later. The total investment was estimated at about $600,000. Even more impressive is that Shone was also juggling military service and university studies while managing much of the construction from thousands of kilometers away. According to the report, hard times helped shape Shone’s resolve. Her mother died when she was 11, which changed her childhood significantly. She grew up helping her father with jobs around the family farm, before finding work mucking out horse stables at an equestrian facility at Drouin West when she was about 14 or 15. Later, she worked in retail at Horseland and found other ways to grow her savings. One unusual investment was in cattle, where she bought a cow and her twin calves for about $1,200 and later sold the younger animals for about $2,500. And while saving meant sacrifices that many teenagers might find hard, Shone eschewed expensive social outings, big shopping trips, buying a car and overseas travel, choosing instead to work or find more work.Purchasing land rather than a pre-owned homeBy the time she was 18, Shone had saved enough money to buy a block of land. She had researched the local market and decided it would be more financially advantageous to build new than to buy an existing home. It was also hard to find anyone who would take her seriously. Shone contacted several real estate agents looking for the right property but found some dismissed her because of her age. The house was built by Metricon and the Crownlee estate team at Warragul was among the groups to back her plans.Building a house from 3000 kilometers awayShone joined the Australian Defense Force after finishing Year 12. Now based at an air force base in the Northern Territory, she works as a chef and studies law part-time. Although she was more than 3,000 kilometers away from the building site, she stayed in touch with the building process over the phone. She corresponded online with Metricon, making design decisions including bathroom tile colors, mostly by email. Her father also provided practical support throughout the project with property visits when required. Metricon’s regional Gippsland sales team said Shone’s readiness, commitment and maturity are why she was able to successfully complete the build.First property and bigger ambitionsShone, who was in Warragul recently to collect the keys to her finished investment property. She doesn’t plan to live in the four-bedroom house. Instead she will rent it out and use it as a stepping stone to a bigger property portfolio. Her next target is to buy another investment property and she hopes to build a few more properties in the future. For Shone, the journey says a lot about what disciplined saving, hard work and long-term planning can do. Her story additionally emphasizes the sacrifices she had to make from her teenage years on to reach her first big financial milestone. More than just a home has been built at 19. She has paved the way for the investment future she began planning at 16.Images Courtesy: Real Estate (dot) comCatch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'This well is not to be built over': A California ranch was warned 20 years ago; young teens are now suffering from a rare cancer
articles.summary: US News: Ladera Ranch is a 4,000-acre planned community in southern Orange County, California. As per the 2020 census, this ranch had a population of 26,170. T.
articles.body: Ladera Ranch is a 4,000-acre planned community in southern Orange County, California. As per the 2020 census, this ranch had a population of 26,170. The residents of the ranch have now raised a cancer concern with the California Department of Public Health that children or young adults of the ranch are suffering from Ewing sarcoma, a very rare cancer that starts in bone or soft tissue. About 2.9 out of every 1 million kids get Ewing sarcoma each year in the US, but the number for Orange County is 3.1.At least six cases of Ewing sarcoma were reported between 2013 and 2024. “There definitely is cause for concern for members of this community,” Dr Janet Yoon, a pediatric hematologist-oncologist at City of Hope who specializes in Ewing sarcoma, said to the Los Angeles Times.Parents believe there is something wrong in the ranchLA Times spoke to Ladera Ranch resident Bonnie Regan, whose son Ryan died of this cancer in October 2025. Ryan was diagnosed with this cancer in 2017 when he was 29. He fought the cancer for eight years until it spread to his lungs, shoulder, brain, spine, lymph node, adrenal gland and stomach. "There is something wrong here. I had never even heard of this kind of cancer before," Regan said.With the growing number of cancer cases, the residents formed a group called Ladera Health Watch to gather health data. Initially, they focused on limiting pesticide use. Now they are concerned that the ranch sits on old oil and gas wells and probably that might have a connection with the cancer cases.'This well is not to be built over'The construction of the ranch began in 1998, and it was completed in 2006. Underneath the ranch are two abandoned oil wells but neither of them had a history of producing oil or gas. These wells were closed twice and the safety standards were checked.The LA Times report said that some residents are concerned that one of the wells may not have been resealed to today's standards. They have also found a handwritten note that said: "This well is not to be built over without further consideration". But it provided no explanation for the warning."Active and abandoned oil and gas wells can spread carcinogens such as benzene, volatile organic compounds and radioactive material into surrounding soil, water and air. Proximity to wells has been linked with elevated rates of childhood leukemia and lymphoma," the LA Times report said.Kenneth Henderson, the supervisor, who wrote the note at that time said he did not recall why he added the warning, but “the well plugging may not have been up to the current standards.”California Geologic Energy Management Division spokesperson said CalGEM generally recommends that structures not be placed over sealed wells. Though wells which are plugged and sealed to current requirements are less likely to experience leakage, there is no guarantee, a spokesperson said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Is the US already losing to China on innovation, logistics and rapid resupply?
articles.summary: "An Army Marches on its Stomach" takes new meaning as the USS Abraham Lincoln deployment exposes critical military supply chain vulnerabilities.
articles.body: It has been said that "An Army Marches on its Stomach." True enough. But even the task of quickly and properly feeding hundreds of thousands of military personnel to keep them battle ready, comes down to some form of logistics, innovation and speed. The recent "controversy" involving USS Abraham Lincoln during its 250-plus day deployment serves as a timely example of that truth. To be sure, many of the accusations made regarding the lack of food and low morale among the sailors were exaggerated by some commentators who harbor a strong dislike of President Donald Trump and were seeking to use the long deployment as a way to embarrass the president and his administration. That acknowledged, there also is an element of "Your side, my side and the truth somewhere in the middle" associated with the resupply and morale issue connected with USS Abraham Lincoln. CENTCOM COMMANDER TOUTS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN MENTAL HEALTH RECORD AFTER MORE THAN 260 DAYS WITHOUT PORT CALL Logistics, innovation and rapid resupply do matter. Be it food, basic staples, weapons systems, or medical supplies. All politics aside, at the very least, the resupply issue surrounding USS Abraham Lincoln — no matter the actual severity — can serve as a very valuable lesson going forward. "Watch the pennies and the dollars will take care of themselves," — a phrase often attributed to Benjamin Franklin — most especially proves true with our military. If the logistics chain breaks or dramatically slows down at the bottom, the warfighting — and winning — capability at the top will suffer… or fail. AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX What constitutes a "penny" for our military? Meaning, what is something which may seem so insignificant and tiny that it never enters the mind of the civilian population — or worse, our "decision makers" — but could prove a game changer for the military if either exponentially innovated and put into action, or because it aged out, failed or was made irrelevant by the technology implemented by our adversaries? A recent conversation with a general opened my eyes to just one such "penny" that is off virtually everyone's radar screen. That being a rivet. The simple rivet. Ironically, about the same size as the penny we need to "watch" if we hope to grow our wealth. INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE More specifically, the general outlined the constant and increasing need to replace old rivets in military (and commercial) aircraft. To be honest, rivets, and more specifically, their replacement on aircraft never entered my mind in all my years until the general informed me not only how vital it was to the maintenance of our fleet and military readiness, while also stating they had fortunately identified a state-of-the-art technology which can do it 15 times faster and more efficiently via robotics. "What’s the big deal," some might understandably ask until one stops to realize that there are collectively hundreds of millions of rivets on military and commercial aircraft which either age out or crack. Faster, cheaper, better and safer is a real advantage. A technology the general informed me, the People’s Republic of China is already employing with its exponentially advancing AI and Robotics platforms. INSIDE CHINA’S AI ‘WOLF PACK’ DRONES BUILT WITH TAIWAN CONFLICT IN MIND Aside from their innovation in rivet replacement, a recent peek into just one of China’s robotic advancements was referenced on this site under the headline: "Chinese humanoid robot breaks Usain Bolt's 100m dash record at 9.39 seconds." Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident who witnessed the record-breaking robotic feat said in part: "At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans. But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look." The Chinese educator spoke the one word which should strike fear into the hearts of all those in charge of safeguarding our national and economic security: "Unstoppable." That one word should — and must — force our decision makers to ask the most critical question of all regarding this topic: "Is the United States losing the innovation, logistics and rapid resupply war to China in our military and commercial sectors?" Fortunately, it appears that question is being asked across the U.S. national and economic security spectrum. As mentioned in the piece, "The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from China, which makes the majority of the world's humanoid robots." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION To this point, President Donald Trump's Federal Communications Commission (FCC) stressed in part: "I welcome these Executive Branch national security determinations, and I am pleased that the FCC has now added foreign-produced advanced robotics and power inverters to the FCC’s Covered List. Following President Trump’s leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains and, with today’s action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that." "Critical supply chains." Be it the replacement of rivets; prompt resupply of food or logistical materials; or actual robots performing any task faster, cheaper and more efficiently than U.S. citizens, our nation can’t afford to fall behind China when it comes to the innovation which drives these endeavors. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP To that end, we had better watch the innovation "pennies" so our national and economic security "dollars" can protect us all.

articles.title: Can Iran use rockets to mine the Strait of Hormuz, as US claims?
articles.summary: Analysts say it’s implausible but Iran is well-versed in adapting conventional weapons to suit its needs.
articles.body:
The United States broke a one-month lull in its war on Iran by striking military targets on Larak Island on Sunday, in what US officials claim was a bid to prevent Tehran from using rockets to deploy sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

The strikes were aimed at Iranian rocket launchers positioned on Larak Island in the strait. The US called the strikes a “limited, precise action” against mine-laying forces.

Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said the US military, which is currently blockading Iranian ports in and around Hormuz, had observed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines.

Iran’s leaders condemned the attack as an “act of aggression” and the IRGC has since launched retaliatory attacks on two US army bases in Jordan. In a statement, the IRGC said its members and civilians were killed in the US strikes. The semi-official Tasnim news agency said at least two people were killed and two injured.

But can mines really be laid using rockets? Here’s what we know.

Can sea mines be launched into the sea using rockets?

Harlan Ullman, a retired senior US naval officer, told Al Jazeera that the US’s claim of rocket-launched mines was “implausible”. He suggested that the US may have received intelligence that Iran was prepared to use launchers from ships to deploy new mines but wanted to downplay the threat.

“It would strike me that a rocket, when it impacts in the water…the impact would be such that it would do a lot of damage to the mines,” Ullman said.

“They (Iran) have got a lot of options they could use to plant these mines. So I would like to know from CENTCOM why they think Iran was using rockets, which to me is very, very novel.”

But Iran has itself advertised its ability to use missiles to lay sea mines.

In January 2025, Iranian state television appeared to show the IRGC using the Fajr-5 Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS) to lay mines during naval exercises.

It is a medium-range system primarily built to fire rockets with warheads and is mounted on trucks which can handle difficult terrain.

Usually, mines are deployed using specialised surface warships, submarines or aircraft. They can be dropped to the seabed or moored slightly above the bottom, waiting to detect the magnetic signature or vibration of passing ships before detonating. Mines can also be positioned to bob just beneath the water surface, exploding when they come in contact with vessels.

Iran is believed to have relied on its hoard of fast, small attack boats to drop an unknown number of explosives into the Hormuz waters before quickly speeding away. Many of these vessels have been struck by the US military.

Last week, US President Donald Trump said CENTCOM had completed mine sweeping in the Strait of Hormuz, clearing it of mines. He warned Iran that ships or boats deploying new mines would be destroyed.

To clear Hormuz of mines to make it safe for general shipping, CENTCOM would have needed to launch a painstakingly slow operation to find and trigger controlled detonations of every single mine, experts say. The US Navy typically uses its Avenger-class mine destroyers for mine sweeping operations as they’re built with materials that make their magnetic vibrations less detectable.

What do we know about Iran’s Fajr-5 rocket system?

Iran has long been known for its innovation in low-cost, high-impact tactics or asymmetric warfare .

In January last year, according to Iranian news reports, the IRGC revealed a new sea mine-laying tactic during a naval exercise using the Fajr-5 MLRS from onshore to scatter mines in the sea.

Analysts at the time called it “innovative” but also “concerning” as it meant the IRGC could now send thousands of mines over vast areas of water with a single launch.

First developed in the 1990s, the Fajr-5 is a 333mm medium-range rocket system typically used to launch artillery rockets.

The system can fire up to four artillery rockets from a mobile, multi-tube truck system. Each rocket is loaded with a 175kg fragmentation warhead designed to shatter into several fast-moving shrapnel fragments that can hit multiple targets. It has a firing range of about 75km (47 miles) and has primarily been used by ground forces to target airfields and military bases.

But the 75km range also means that if deployed to lay sea mines, the Fajr-5 could cover the entire Strait of Hormuz.

Newer variants, such as the Fajr-5c, are equipped with highly precise navigation systems and can fire rockets up to 130km (81 miles).

How could Fajr-5 be used to lay sea mines?

Iran has not confirmed that the Fajr-5 or any other rocket system is currently being used to deploy sea mines.

In theory, the rocket’s warhead could be packed with sea mines, rather than explosives, as appeared to be demonstrated in the IRGC’s naval exercise in January 2025.

Once launched from a truck on the coast, the mine-laden rockets would fly over targeted naval coordinates and open their casings mid-air.

Unexploded sea mines would then be released into the air and dropped into the ocean. Attached to them would be small parachutes or other materials designed to slow their drop and allow for a soft landing, preventing them from detonating when they hit water.

Once in the water, the mines would sink to the seabed or float under the surface.

A single rocket launch could technically carry dozens, if not hundreds, of sea mines, spreading them across the narrow Strait of Hormuz.

Such a tactic could overwhelm minesweeping operations, while keeping Iran’s fast boats from being attacked by CENTCOM forces.

Who has aerial mine-laying capabilities?

According to the US Navy , it already uses aircraft and launchers to deploy Quickstrike mines into the sea. This is a shallow-water mine made with a 2,000lb (907kg) bomb fitted with mine components, wing and tail kits for rapid mid-range precision delivery by US Navy and US Air Force warplanes. They can be launched over a range of 25km (40 miles) from beyond enemy air defences.

Modern variants use Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM) to enable aircraft to release mines with greater precision from much higher altitudes. According to the US Navy , JDAM is a guidance kit that can be added to an existing unguided bomb to turn it into a precision-guided, “smart” munition.

So far, the US has used this tactic in training and testing exercises only, most recently in April, when the US Navy said it had tested a new guided munition, known as the GBU-75, capable of striking naval targets or deploying sea mines from aircraft hundreds of kilometres away.

Experts say the US needs to speed up development of new ways to place mines in the sea, including by launching them from land.

Writing for the US Naval Institute last year, US Navy Commander Adam Pace wrote: “It remains imperative to find a solution that can facilitate mine warfare while achieving survivability, desired volume and speed of delivery. Land-launched naval mining builds on established units and systems, such as Marine littoral regiments and the Army’s multidomain task forces, to expand the ability of land-based units to influence the maritime domain”.
